cop-b1-setup-and-quality-completions.walkthrough:
Dana is a junior developer at a small fintech startup, and her ticket for the day is to add a monthly-payment calculator to the loan application form. She's used Cursor's Tab autocomplete before without thinking much about it, but this is her first time trying to use it deliberately.

She opens the real file where the calculator will live, not a blank scratch file, since the surrounding code already imports the currency-formatting helpers she'll need — and Cursor's codebase index can see the rest of the project too. She types a descriptive function name, calculateMonthlyPayment, and above it writes a three-line comment stating the inputs, what happens when the interest rate is zero, and that the result should be rounded to two decimal places. Then she types the opening brace and waits.

Grey ghost text appears: a full function body that converts the annual rate to a monthly decimal, applies the standard formula, and returns a rounded number. She doesn't press Tab immediately — she reads it first, and notices it doesn't check for the zero-rate case she mentioned in her comment. She deletes the suggestion, adds an explicit EDGE CASE line to her comment, and retriggers. The next suggestion includes the check, matching her comment exactly. She accepts it with Tab.

Before moving on, she pastes a follow-up into Cursor Chat: write 3 test cases — a normal case, the zero-rate edge case, and a term of 1 month. It returns three test cases with expected values, which she runs against her new function — all three pass.

From opening the file to a passing test suite: about six minutes. Dana ships the function in her next commit, able to explain exactly what it does because she read every line before accepting it.

cop-i1-copilot-chat-explanation-and-expl.walkthrough:
Priya joined a new team two weeks ago and has been assigned a bug in a module called reconcile.ts that nobody currently on her team wrote. The bug report describes an intermittent crash, and she suspects it'll take real tracing across multiple files, not a one-line answer — so instead of asking a quick question in Cursor Chat, she decides this is worth a dedicated investigation and opens a fresh Claude Code session pointed at the repo.

She tells it plainly not to edit anything, then asks about the 40-line function the bug report points to, with three specific follow-ups: what happens if the items array is empty, whether the function mutates its input, and where else in the file it's called without checking the return value for null. She picked those three because empty-input and null-return bugs are the most common causes of an intermittent crash like the one described.

Claude Code responds with a paragraph on the transformation logic, then confirms directly: an empty items array returns an empty result without throwing, the array is copied rather than mutated, but two call sites elsewhere in the file call the function without checking whether it returned null.

Priya doesn't take this as fact. She opens the file herself and reads the two flagged call sites — both really do skip the null check, and one matches the exact conditions in the bug report. She fixes that call site, adds a null check, and writes a one-line test to prevent regression.

Before closing the ticket, she asks for a three-sentence summary she can paste into the PR description. From opening the session to a verified root cause and a written note for reviewers: about eleven minutes — and the next person who touches reconcile.ts won't have to redo any of it.

cop-i2-edit-across-files-with-copilot.walkthrough:
Tom is a backend engineer at a mid-size e-commerce company, and his task for the sprint is adding order cancellation — a feature that needs a new API route, new business logic, and new test coverage. It touches business rules he's not entirely sure about yet, so he decides he wants to watch it happen rather than hand it off unattended, and opens Cursor Agent instead of a Codex cloud task.

He pastes a scoped description: add a cancel endpoint, name the two files that should change, explicitly say not to touch the database schema or add dependencies, state the business rule that only pending or processing orders can be cancelled, otherwise return a 409, and ask for three specific test cases.

Cursor responds first with a short plan — it will add a cancelOrder method to the service, wire a new route, and write the three requested tests. Tom reads the plan and confirms it matches what he asked before it starts writing.

A minute later, three file diffs appear. He reviews them one at a time: the service method's status check looks correct, the route wiring matches the existing route style, and the tests cover the valid-cancel, invalid-status, and not-found cases as requested. He accepts each file individually rather than approving the whole batch at once.

He runs the test suite himself afterward — all three new tests pass, plus the existing suite is untouched. From opening Agent to a committed, reviewed change: about eighteen minutes. He notes for next time that the same task, once he trusts the business rule, would be a fine candidate to hand to a Codex cloud task instead and walk away from entirely.

cop-a1-coding-agent-issue-to-pull-reques.walkthrough:
Aisha is an engineering manager at a logistics startup, and she's just noticed the public search endpoint has no rate limiting — a real risk since one misbehaving client could degrade the service for everyone. Rather than pull an engineer off their current sprint work, she decides to delegate it.

She opens a new GitHub issue and writes it like a spec: a one-paragraph problem statement, four numbered acceptance criteria covering a per-key request limit, a 429 response with a Retry-After header, a configurable limit, and three named test cases, plus an explicit scope line naming the two files that should change and the existing Redis client to reuse instead of adding anything new. She connects the repo at chatgpt.com/codex and hands the issue to a new cloud task.

About fifteen minutes later, a draft PR appears. Its description restates each acceptance criterion and says how it was addressed. Aisha reads the diff the same way she'd review a new hire's first PR: she checks the Redis counter logic isn't vulnerable to a race condition under concurrent requests, confirms the 429 response actually includes a correctly formatted Retry-After header, and runs through all three test cases to confirm they test what they claim to.

She finds one gap — the environment variable has no documented default, so a missing config value would silently disable rate limiting. She leaves a PR comment describing the issue. The task picks up the comment and pushes a fix within a few minutes, adding a sane default and a test for the missing-config case.

Aisha merges once CI is green and every acceptance criterion checks out — a real feature delegated and reviewed in under an hour of her own attention, most of which was writing the issue itself.

cop-a2-ai-code-review-on-github.walkthrough:
Ben is a tech lead at a subscription-billing company, and a mid-level engineer on his team just opened a PR adding an order-cancellation endpoint. Before Ben looks at it himself, he wants a fast first pass. The repo already has Codex enabled as an automatic PR reviewer, so he adds a comment naming three specific worries: whether the authorization check runs before the status check, whether the Redis-based rate counter has a race condition, and whether any new error response leaks internal details.

He picked those three because they're the categories of bug that have actually caused incidents on his team before — a generic review request tends to return mostly style comments, so he briefs it the way he'd brief a new reviewer joining the team.

A few minutes later — longer than a simple diff scan, because this review actually executes parts of the code — three comments appear. The first confirms the authorization check does run first. The second flags a real issue: the Redis increment and the limit check aren't wrapped in a single atomic operation, so two simultaneous requests near the limit could both slip through. The third confirms the error responses are clean.

Ben doesn't take the race-condition flag on faith. He opens the file, reads the two lines in question, and agrees — it's a real check-then-act race. He leaves a review comment asking the original author to wrap both operations in a single atomic transaction.

He still does his own full read of the diff afterward, and still asks a second human teammate to review before merge, since this touches business logic. But the AI pass caught a real concurrency bug in under five minutes, and it took him two minutes to write the review request that made that catch possible.

cop-a3-custom-instructions-for-your-repo.walkthrough:
Sofia is a tech lead on a five-person team sharing one Next.js repository, and she's noticed every developer's AI suggestions look slightly different depending on which of the three tools they used — some produce old Pages Router patterns, some invent a new error-handling style each time. None of it matches the conventions the team actually agreed on in code review over the past year, and worse, three different people had each started their own half-written instructions file for their own tool.

She consolidates them into one AGENTS.md at the repository root — the file Codex reads automatically and Cursor reads as ambient project context. She states the stack precisely — TypeScript 5.x, Next.js 15 with the App Router, no Pages Router code — instead of just naming the framework. She adds three positive conventions, each pointing at a real file: all API responses use the shared ApiResult type, errors are thrown as AppError subclasses, and database queries go through a repository layer rather than inline Prisma calls. She adds a short 'Do not' section: no new dependencies without approval, no third-party date libraries since the team standardized on the native Temporal API, and no unrelated schema changes.

In CLAUDE.md, she deletes the team's old duplicate content and replaces it with a single line: `@AGENTS.md`. For one legacy directory that genuinely still uses the Pages Router, she adds a scoped .cursor/rules/legacy.mdc with a globs pattern so Cursor only applies the old-style guidance there.

To check it's working, she asks the same ordinary question — add an endpoint that returns order data — in Cursor, Claude Code, and Codex. All three wrap the response in ApiResult, throw an OrderNotFoundError extending AppError, and call into an orders repository method, without her mentioning any of those conventions in the question itself. Total setup time: about twenty-five minutes, for three tools that now agree with each other.

cop-a4-integrating-copilot-into-a-team-w.walkthrough:
Grace is an engineering director at a company where individual teams picked their own AI coding tools with no coordination — some engineers live in Cursor, others swear by Claude Code, and one team has been quietly running Codex cloud tasks on their own initiative. Nobody has a shared source of truth for which tool to reach for, and she's just found out one engineer's unattended agent task touched a repo it had no business being in.

She starts by writing the one-page policy: Cursor as the default for hands-on daily coding, Claude Code for deep investigation and CI-integrated review, and Codex cloud tasks for well-scoped, walk-away-able delegation. She names the actual repos that unattended tasks are allowed to touch — three low-risk internal tools to start — and states plainly that everything else stays hands-on-only until a lead explicitly adds it.

She points every repo at a shared AGENTS.md, imported into CLAUDE.md with `@AGENTS.md`, so the policy is encoded in the tools themselves and not just a document people forget.
